Gravity is like a giant, gentle hug the Earth gives to you, me, trees, houses, and even the air. It pulls us all down towards its big, round tummy (the very middle of the Earth). Because Earth is so incredibly big and strong, its hug is very powerful, and that's why our feet stay stuck on the ground and we don't float off into space like a balloon! It's always pulling us down, keeping us safe and sound right here.

title: How is yeast harvested?

title: How does an audio equalizer actually WORK? (Not how do I use one)
text: Imagine your music is like a big, yummy cake, but instead of just one flavor, it has lots of different flavors all mixed together! Some parts of the cake are really deep and rumbling, like a big chocolate chunk (we call these 'bass' sounds). Other parts are super high and sparkly, like sprinkles (we call these 'treble' sounds). And lots of other sounds are in the middle, like the main cake part. An equalizer is like a special set of magic spoons that lets you pick out just one flavor of the cake and make it taste stronger or weaker. If you want more of the big chocolate chunk sounds, you use that spoon to make them louder! If you want less of the sparkly sprinkle sounds, you use another spoon to make them quieter. It doesn't add new flavors to the cake, it just changes how much you taste of the flavors that are already there, so you can make your music taste (or sound!) just right for your ears!

They *hate* this special house! It's too sour or too weird for them, so they don't want to come in. They run away! So, the friendly helper bacteria, who were already hanging around, see this amazing new house made just for them. They rush inside, eat all their favorite food, and start having a big party! They invite all their friendly helper friends, and soon there are so many good bacteria in the house that there's no room for any grumpy bullies. They keep the food safe and make it taste yummy, like pickles or yogurt!

All its weight just hangs down like a heavy blanket, and you have to lift *all* of it, and it feels like a big, squishy blob that's hard to get a hold of. But if that teddy bear suddenly came alive and tried to help you by making its body a little bit stiff, like when you make your own body stiff to jump, it would be much easier to pick up! So, when a body is limp, it's not actually heavier, it just feels that way because it's not helping you *at all*, and all the weight is floppy and hard to gather up, which makes it feel super, super heavy for you to lift!

title: What is falsetto, and how is it different from normal singing?
text: Okay, imagine your regular singing voice is like when you talk normally, but you make it pretty with music! It feels strong and comes from your chest. Now, imagine you're trying to make a tiny, squeaky mouse sound, or sing super, super high like a little bird flying way up in the sky! That very light, airy, and high voice, almost like it's floating out of your head, is called falsetto. It's different because it doesn't feel as big or strong as your regular singing voice; it's like your voice is tiptoeing on the highest notes!

title: How is Planet Earth the series filmed?

They use very special "seeing boxes" (we call them cameras) that are like super-duper eyes that can take pictures and make movies. They put these seeing boxes on tall sticks, on flying toys called drones that go up in the sky, or even on special little cars or boats that go underwater. The people have to be super patient, like waiting a very, very long time for a cookie, just to see an animal do something cool! They also have special "listening ears" (microphones) to record all the sounds, like birds singing or water splashing. After they get all the pictures and sounds, they put it all together like a big, exciting puzzle to make the show you watch!

If your eyes need a bit of help to see things far away, like the TV, your glasses just make everything clear and easy to see. It's like putting on your comfy shoes to walk – it helps you walk better, it doesn't make your feet worse. Your eyes might change a little bit as you grow bigger, but that's just a normal part of growing up, not because of watching TV or wearing your special seeing-helpers. So, just enjoy seeing everything clearly!

title: what's the difference between controlling the volume on the PC and controlling the volume on its speakers?
text: Imagine your computer is like a little singer, and your speakers are like a big megaphone that makes the singer's voice bigger for everyone to hear. When you change the volume on your computer, it's like telling the singer to sing quieter or louder herself – she can whisper or sing really loud. When you change the volume on your speakers, it's like turning a knob on the big megaphone. If the singer (computer) is already whispering, the megaphone can only make that whisper a little bit louder, but it won't ever sound like she's shouting. If the singer is already singing loudly, the megaphone can make that loud singing even *more* loud! So, your computer decides how loud the sound *starts*, and your speakers decide how much bigger or smaller to make that sound when it comes out for your ears.

It's like your body is trying to protect itself from the pain that the mean bug is causing in your throat when you try to drink.

title: Why is it harder to kick a football farther in cold weather versus warm?
text: Imagine the air is like a big swimming pool! When it's super cold outside, the air in our "pool" gets a little thicker, like trying to run through mud instead of just water. So, when you kick the football, it has to push harder through that thicker, colder air, which slows it down faster. Also, the football itself gets a bit stiff and hard when it's cold, kind of like your bouncy ball gets less bouncy when it's been in the cold for a while. A stiff ball doesn't squish and spring off your foot with as much power, so it doesn't get that extra "oomph" to fly super far. When it's warm, the air is lighter and the ball is nice and squishy, so it bounces off your foot easily and flies much farther!

title: Why instant coffee is water soluble, but coffee grounds aren't?
text: Imagine you have some yummy chocolate milk powder (that's like instant coffee). Someone already made chocolate milk, and then they took all the water out, so it's just the dry, yummy part left. When you put it in water, it remembers how to be chocolate milk right away and dissolves into your drink! Now, imagine you have a whole chocolate bar (that's like coffee grounds). If you just put the solid chocolate bar in water, it won't magically turn into chocolate milk. It's still a solid piece, and all the yummy chocolate flavor is stuck inside. You'd have to melt it or break it into super tiny pieces and stir for a long, long time to get some chocolatey water. So, instant coffee has already had all its yummy coffee flavor taken out and dried into a powder, making it super easy to mix with water again, but coffee grounds are still like the whole chocolate bar, with all the yummy flavor still stuck inside its little pieces!

title: Why does Coke (or any soda) taste a lot sweeter when it’s at room temperature, compared to when it’s cold?

Because they're sleepy, they don't notice all the sweet sugar in the Coke as much. But when the Coke gets warm, those little taste bud helpers wake up and get super excited! They start working really hard and notice *all* the sweetness, making the soda taste much, much sweeter to you. It's like turning up the volume on a sweet song!

text: Okay, imagine you have a magnet, and it has a special invisible "pulling power," right? Now, imagine that pulling power isn't just sitting still. It feels warm and special, maybe because the brain is trying to make a nice, calm picture for someone who is very, very tired, just before they might go to sleep for good. title: How can you determine the location of a fault line by just looking at a topographical map?

When this happens, the hills and valleys on one side of the crack don't quite line up perfectly with the hills and valleys on the other side anymore. So, if you look super carefully at your map, you might see where the lines for a hill suddenly stop and then start again a little bit further along, or where a straight river suddenly makes a sharp turn, or where the lines showing the height of the land look all squished or broken in a straight line. It's like if you had a drawing of a road, and someone ripped the paper and moved one side a little – the road wouldn't connect perfectly anymore! That broken or offset pattern on the map is a big clue that there's a fault line hiding underneath.

title: Why do people wake up at 3am? What's so special about it?
text: Sometimes, grown-ups (and even kids!) wake up when it's still super dark outside, like at 3 AM, and it feels a bit weird because everyone else is sleeping! It's not because 3 AM is a magic number or has special powers. It's mostly because our bodies have a special 'sleep clock' inside them. This clock usually tells us when to feel sleepy and when to wake up. When we sleep, we don't just stay super deeply asleep all night. Our sleep comes in waves, like the ocean! Sometimes we're in really deep sleep, and sometimes we're in lighter sleep. When we're in a lighter sleep wave, it's much easier for little things to wake us up. Maybe we need to go pee-pee, or we heard a tiny noise, or we had a funny dream, or sometimes our brain just decides to think about something for a bit. It's totally normal for our bodies to have these little wake-ups during the night, especially during those lighter sleep times. Usually, after a little while, our body clock just gently tells us to go back to sleep until the sun comes up again!

title: How can we talk about the universe being flat? Is it not expanding in all directions?
text: Imagine our universe is like a super, super giant bedsheet that goes on forever, not like a pancake you can pick up, but like a flat floor you can walk on. When we say the universe is "flat," it means if you drew two perfectly straight lines next to each other on this giant floor, they would always stay the same distance apart and never get closer or further away, like on a perfectly flat playground. It doesn't have big bumps or curves like a giant ball or a wavy blanket. Now, imagine this giant bedsheet is also always getting bigger and bigger everywhere, like someone is gently pulling on all its edges at the same time. That's the "expanding in all directions" part! Even though it's getting bigger, its *shape* or *kind of floor* stays flat, it doesn't puff up into a ball or get all wrinkly. So, it's a flat floor that's just getting bigger and bigger all the time.

title: why are elements measured in half life instead of full life?
text: Imagine you have a big pile of special magic LEGO bricks that like to just poof away and turn into different kinds of LEGO bricks all by themselves! If you pick just *one* of these magic bricks, you can never ever know *exactly* when *that one* will decide to poof. It's like trying to guess when one specific bubble will pop – it's a surprise! But, if you look at your *whole big pile* of magic bricks, we *can* tell you how long it will take for *half* of all your bricks to poof away. We use "half-life" because we can reliably tell you when half will be gone, but we can't say when *all* of them will be gone, because some might stick around for a super, super long time, maybe even forever, and never poof! So, half-life is a very helpful way to measure how fast things disappear when we can't guess about just one.

title: What is equity and why is it important?

"Equity" is like making sure *everyone* gets the right number of stools they *need* so *everyone* can see the parade. Maybe the super tall friend doesn't need any stool, the medium friend needs one, and the smallest friend needs two! It's important because it makes sure everyone has a fair chance to play, learn, and be happy, even if they start out a little different. It means giving everyone what they *need* to be successful, so no one feels left out.

The dew point is the special temperature where the air gets just cold enough that it *has* to let go of some of its water, and it starts to make those little drops, like dew on the grass in the morning! So, relative humidity tells you *how much water* is in the air right now compared to what it *could* hold, like how full your invisible sponge is. A "trade war" is like when big countries do this, making it more expensive for things like toys, food, or clothes to come from the other country, and then the other country does it back, like they're having a big argument about sharing their stuff!

title: Why are juices made from concentrate?
text: Imagine you have a super yummy orange, and you squeeze all the juice out. If we want to bring juice from far-away places where lots of oranges grow, it's much easier and cheaper for the big trucks and ships to carry lots and lots of these tiny, squished orange blobs instead of big, heavy jugs of juice. It also helps the juice stay good for a longer time before it gets yucky. Then, when it's time to put it in a carton for you, they just add clean water back in, and poof! If human skin got super, super hot, it would definitely get very dry and hard, like anything that gets really hot and loses all its water, but it wouldn't make the same kind of bubbly, yummy 'crackle' sound you hear from a pig roast because our skin isn't built quite the same for that special crunch.

title: What likely happened to the bodies that were trapped inside the Titanic?

title: Before super basic commodities like soap and toothpaste came about, how did people brush their teeth and get clothes clean?
text: Imagine long, long ago, before the soap you use in the bath or the toothpaste you squish on your brush! title: Why does food that's been heated in a conventional oven or stove pan almost always taste better than when it's heated in a microwave?
text: Imagine your food is like a toy that needs to get warm. When you put it in the oven or a pan on the stove, it's like giving your toy a big, warm hug all over! It makes the water wiggle and get hot really, really fast, which warms up the food quickly. But it doesn't give the outside that special crispy hug or make it brown and toasty, so it often just feels soft and warm, and doesn't get those extra yummy smells and tastes that the oven or pan makes.

title: Why are their different types of pain, for example, dull, sharp etc?

Your brain needs these different kinds of messages so it knows exactly what's happening and how to help you feel better, like knowing if it's just a little bump or something that needs more attention!

title: Why can't any of my electronics use multiple channels/sources (e.g. wifi & 4g) to download data at the same time?
text: Imagine your phone wants to get a big box of new toys (that's your data, like a video or a game!). It has two different ways to get them: one is like a super-fast friend who lives very close and brings toys from your house (that's Wi-Fi), and the other is a friend who can go anywhere but might be a little slower because they come from far away (that's 4G). Your phone's little brain is very good at telling *one* friend to go get *all* the toys from *one* place. It's like it has one special door where all the toy pieces come in, and it wants them to come in order so they fit together perfectly. If it tried to tell both friends to bring different parts of the *same* toy box at the same time, it would get very messy and confusing, and the pieces might not fit together right when they arrive! So, your phone just picks the best and fastest friend to bring *all* the toys from *one* place, so everything arrives perfectly and in order.

title: How a song you used to know, but after 10 years are unable to say a single phrase from it, once the music starts you suddenly can sing the whole thing without even thinking?

title: Why do we feel nauseated when we try to read in a moving vehicle?

It's like one part of your brain says "still!" and another part says "moving!" When your brain gets that mixed up, it sometimes thinks, "Uh oh, maybe we ate something yucky that's making us confused!" title: I have a portable air conditioner. Is it more effective to direct the vents towards the floor or ceiling to cool a room?

So, if you point your chilly blanket-maker (the AC) *up towards the ceiling*, the cold air will float out, then naturally start to fall down and spread all around the room, pushing the warm air up and making everything nice and cool. If you point it at the floor, it just makes a cold spot right there, and doesn't get to spread its cool magic everywhere as well. So, aim high for a super cool room!

title: Why do we have the Statute of Limitations? Why do we let people go, just because they committed crimes in the past?
text: Imagine you lost your favorite toy a super long time ago. It would be really, really hard to remember exactly where you left it, right? And maybe some of the clues, like a drawing you made of it, are gone now. That's a bit like why we have a rule called the 'Statute of Limitations' for grown-up rules. It means that after a certain amount of time, like many, many sleeps, the grown-ups stop trying to figure out if someone broke a rule a super long time ago. We don't really 'let them go' because we want to, but because it gets super hard to remember exactly what happened and find all the clues from so long ago. People might forget important things, and it's not really fair to make someone worry forever and ever about something that happened ages ago, especially if they've been good ever since. So, it helps us focus on what's happening now and be fair to everyone.

title: What is the difference between an oligarchy and an aristocracy?
text: Okay, imagine your class has a special club, and only a few kids get to make all the rules for everyone. If those few kids are in charge because they are the strongest, or they have the most toys, or they are just really good at telling everyone what to do right now, that's like an **oligarchy**. It's just a small group that's powerful. But if those few kids are in charge because their mommies and daddies, and their grandmas and grandpas, were *always* the ones in charge, or they have really old, fancy names that everyone knows, that's like an **aristocracy**. It's still a small group, but they are in charge because of who their family is, like they were born into the "rule-making" family.

title: What prevents clouds with water freezing up into an ice ball and falling onto our heads?
text: Clouds are actually made of super-duper tiny little water sprinkles or even tiny ice sprinkles, much, much smaller than a grain of sugar! Even when it's super cold high up in the sky, these tiny sprinkles are just too small and too far apart to hold hands and make one giant, heavy ice ball that would fall down and bonk us on the head. Instead, they just float around with the wind because they're so light, and when they do get a *little* bit bigger, they fall as gentle rain or soft snow, not a big thump!

title: What determines whether a person sleeps on their back, side, or stomach? Is it just habit? Can we change the position we sleep in over time?
text: Imagine your bed is a big, soft cloud, and your body wants to find the comfiest spot on it! How you sleep – on your back like a superhero flying, on your side like a curled-up kitty, or on your tummy like you're hugging the bed – is mostly because your body just *likes* that spot the best. It feels good and safe and cozy to you. A lot of it is just like having a favorite way to sit on the couch or a favorite toy you always hold a certain way; your body just gets into a habit of doing what feels right. But guess what? You totally *can* change it! It's like learning a new game or trying a new food. It might feel a little strange at first, but if you try to lie a different way, maybe with a pillow helping you stay there, your body can learn to feel comfy in that new spot too. It just takes a little time for your body to get used to the new cozy position, and then that new way can become your favorite habit!

title: Why do we feel extreme chronic pain? Wouldn't a little pain feel good but it seems like a chronic pain would lower our survival skills
text: Imagine your body has a special alarm system, just like the smoke alarm in your house. When you accidentally touch something hot, or trip and fall, a little beep goes off to say "Hey! Be careful! Something is wrong here!" That little beep helps you learn what not to do so you stay safe. But sometimes, if something is really, really wrong, like if you hurt your leg badly, that alarm goes super loud and won't stop ringing! That's extreme pain, and it's your body yelling "HELP! This is a big problem!" Now, imagine that alarm just keeps ringing and ringing and ringing, even after the problem is fixed, or even if the alarm just got stuck and won't turn off. That's chronic pain. It's not supposed to feel good, because it's always a warning! And you're super smart, because when that alarm is stuck on super loud all the time, it makes it really hard to play, or run, or even think clearly, which isn't helpful at all. It's like the alarm system got a little bit broken and is making too much noise when it shouldn't.

title: What's the connection between entropy and the end of the universe ?
text: Imagine your playroom is super neat, with all your toys in their boxes. That's like the beginning of the universe, very organized! Entropy is just a fancy word for how things naturally get messy and spread out. If you play with your toys, they get all over the floor, right? That's entropy happening! The universe is also getting messier and more spread out over a super, super long time. Stars burn out, galaxies move further apart, and all the energy that makes things happen slowly spreads out everywhere. When everything is completely spread out and mixed up, like if all your toys were tiny bits of dust sprinkled evenly all over the world, there wouldn't be any more energy to make new stars or even make things move or change. It would be like everything is flat, still, and super boring, with no more light or warmth anywhere. That's what people mean by the "end of the universe" because of entropy – it just means everything will be so spread out and mixed up that nothing exciting can ever happen again.

title: Why do cellphone manufacturers/communication companies recommend that you let a new phone die before recharging it?
text: Okay, imagine your phone has a special tummy for power, like your tummy for food! A long, long time ago, with some *old* kinds of phone tummies, if you kept filling them up when they weren't totally, totally empty, they'd get a bit confused. They might 'forget' how much power they could actually hold and only think they could hold a little bit, even when they could hold more! So, grown-ups used to say to let them get super empty so they'd remember their full size. But guess what? Your new phone has a super-smart tummy that doesn't get confused anymore! It's like a magic tummy that always knows how much power it can hold, no matter when you fill it up. So, you don't need to let your new phone get totally, totally empty; you can charge it whenever it's a little bit hungry!

title: How does shooting lasers (i.e. LASIK) into someone's eyes dramatically improve their vision?
text: Imagine your eye is like a super special camera that takes pictures of the world. Sometimes, the "window" at the very front of your camera eye isn't perfectly shaped, so the pictures you see are a little blurry or fuzzy, like when your toy car is out of focus. When doctors do LASIK, they use a super gentle, super smart light beam, called a laser, to carefully, carefully shave off tiny, tiny bits from that window of your eye. It's like a tiny magic eraser that reshapes the window just a little bit, making it perfectly smooth and just the right curve. When the window is shaped perfectly, your eye camera can take super clear, super sharp pictures again, so everything you look at isn't fuzzy anymore, it's crystal clear!

title: Why do people gasp when they see something shocking or surprising?
text: Imagine your body is like a little car, and your brain is the driver. When you see something really surprising, like a big dog jumping out or a toy suddenly falling, your brain goes 'Whoa! What was that?!' and it quickly tells your body to get ready. To get ready super fast, your body takes a quick, big gulp of air, which is called a gasp! It's like your body is quickly filling up with extra energy-air so it can be super alert and ready to do whatever it needs to do, like run away, jump, or just think really, really fast about what just happened. It's just your body's way of saying, 'Okay, I'm ready!'

title: What do EPA opponents mean when they say they take issue with EPA overreach? What do they mean by EPA overreach?
text: Imagine the EPA is like a special grown-up helper whose job is to make sure our planet stays clean and healthy, like making sure our water is good to drink and the air is nice to breathe. To do this, they make rules, like "don't throw your trash on the ground" or "factories need to clean their smoke." But sometimes, other grown-ups say, "Whoa, EPA! You're making *too many* rules!" or "You're trying to tell people what to do about things that aren't really your job!" When they say "EPA overreach," they mean they think the EPA is trying to be *too big* of a boss, making rules about things they shouldn't, or making rules that are too strict or get in the way too much, even when they're just trying to keep things clean. It's like if your teacher told you exactly how to play with your toys at home, not just at school – some people might say the teacher is "overreaching" their job.

title: How can a ruling in a Washington state court overrule executive action?
text: Okay, imagine your grown-up (that's like the Governor or President) says, "Everyone has to eat broccoli for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, every single day!" That's their special rule, called an "executive action." But then, another grown-up, who is like a "judge" (that's the court), looks at the big rule book for your house (that's like the laws and the Constitution). The judge says, "Wait a minute! The big rule book says grown-ups can make rules, but they can't make rules that are unfair to everyone, or that break *other*, *bigger* rules, like the one that says you need different kinds of food to be healthy, or that you can't just change *all* the meal rules without a good reason." So, even though your grown-up wanted to make that broccoli rule, the judge says, "Nope! That rule can't happen because it doesn't follow the *bigger* rules." And because the judge's job is to make sure everyone follows the *bigger* rules, their decision means your grown-up's special broccoli rule can't be used. That's how a court can say "no" to a special rule from the grown-up who runs things!

title: Why are snow storms with lightning so rare? What prevents them from occurring?
text: Okay, imagine lightning is like a super bouncy ball that needs lots and lots of energy to jump really high and make a spark, which usually happens when the air is warm and full of energy. Snow, though, is like a sleepy little snowflake that only comes out when it's super, super cold, like when you put your ice cream in the freezer. For lightning and snow to happen at the same time, it's like trying to have a super bouncy ball jump really high *inside* a super cold freezer! It's very tricky because usually, if it's cold enough for snow, the air is calm and doesn't have enough warm, bouncy energy to make the lightning sparks. So, you need a very special kind of storm where it's cold for snow, but still has a little pocket of super energetic, bouncy air way up high to make the lightning happen, and that's why it doesn't happen very often!

title: Why does holding your breath / straining seem to help when performing an action, such as benchpressing, of lifting something heavy?
text: Imagine your body is like a tower made of soft blocks. When you try to lift something super heavy, your tower might wobble and fall over! But if you take a deep breath and hold it, and then squeeze your tummy muscles really, really tight (like you're trying to make your belly super hard), you make the *middle* part of your tower super strong and stiff, like a solid, unmoving tree trunk. This makes your whole body firm, like a strong pillar. Now, when you push or lift, your arms and legs have a super strong middle to push *from*, so they can push much harder without your body wobbling. It's like having a strong, sturdy table to push off of, instead of a wobbly jelly table!

title: Why is automaton suddenly a big deal? Hasn't it already been happening for a long time? What's different now?
text: You're super smart for noticing that! Robots and machines that do things by themselves have been around for a long, long time, like your washing machine that cleans clothes or a toy car that drives itself a little bit. That's true! But imagine your old toy car could only go straight or turn one way. Now, it's like we taught that car to drive itself to the store, pick up your favorite snack, and come back home all by itself! These new "automaton" (which is just a fancy word for those smart helpers) are like they went to a super-duper smart school. They can now learn new things really fast, understand what we say, draw pictures, write stories, and even help doctors look at tiny things. They're not just doing simple, repeated jobs anymore; they're doing things that used to need a grown-up's brain, and they're doing it in lots more places, like in our phones, our cars, and even helping to make movies. That's why everyone is talking about them – because they've gotten so much smarter and can do so many amazing, new things that change how we play and work!

title: why do online cable streaming services only show a select 4 or 5 commercials?
text: Imagine you have a big toy box with lots and lots of different toys in it. When you watch regular TV, it's like they have that giant toy box and can pick out all sorts of different toys (commercials) to show you. But when you watch your shows on a tablet or computer, it's like they only have a much smaller toy box! Maybe not as many grown-ups bought space for *their* toys (ads) in that special small box. So, the people who run the shows just show you the few toys they *do* have over and over again. It's also easier for their special TV computer to just remember those few toys and show them to you many times, so you really remember them, instead of trying to find lots of new ones every single time!

title: Why do snakes stick out their tongues so much?
text: Snakes stick out their tongues a lot because that's how they "smell" everything around them! They don't have a nose like you and me to sniff the air. Instead, their super-duper tongue is like a special antenna that picks up tiny, invisible smell messages floating all over the place. When they pull their tongue back into their mouth, they touch it to a special spot inside that helps them figure out what those smells mean. It tells them things like, "Hey, there's a yummy snack hiding over there!" or "Uh oh, there's a big animal close by!" So, they're just trying to figure out what's going on in their world, like you use your eyes to look!

title: Why do Comcast and the big companies fight against net Neutrality? Like wouldn't they make more money in the long run with more consumers and cheaper ads instead of fewer users who are paying more for certain websites?
text:
Imagine the internet is like a super big road where all the cars (that's you visiting websites!) drive.
Net Neutrality is like saying everyone gets to drive on the road at the same speed, no matter if you're a big fancy car or a small little car. No one can make your car go slower or make you pay extra to go faster on the main road.

Now, big companies like Comcast are like the people who *own* the road. They think, "Hmm, what if we could make some cars go super-fast, but only if they pay us extra money? And what if we made other cars go really, really slow, unless *they* pay us extra money too?" They want to be able to charge more money for the "fast lanes" to the websites you like, or even charge *you* more money to use those fast lanes. They believe they can make a lot more money by being able to pick favorites and charge for special treatment, instead of just letting everyone drive equally on the road. They want to be in charge of who gets to go fast and who goes slow, because that gives them a lot of power and they think it will make their piggy bank much, much bigger.

title: Why can we study something for 3 hours and remember nothing, but watch a movie for 3 hours and remember everything?
text: Imagine your brain is like a super-duper special closet for all your memories! When you watch a movie, it's like a big, exciting party with colorful balloons, funny characters, and a super cool story. Your brain loves parties! It takes all those fun, exciting things and puts them neatly into special, sticky boxes in your closet, so it's easy to find them later. But when you study, sometimes it's like looking at a pile of plain, boring socks. There are no pictures, no stories, and it's not super exciting. title: What sense does it make for bats,opossums etc to live upside down?
text: Imagine you're playing hide-and-seek and you climb way, way up high where no one can reach you easily! That's kind of why bats and opossums hang upside down. It keeps them super safe from other animals that walk on the ground, like foxes or cats, because those animals can't climb up there to get them. For bats, it's also like being on a diving board! When they want to fly, they just let go and *whoosh*, they're flying right away, which is easier than trying to run and then fly with their little legs. Opossums have super strong tails that are like an extra hand to hold onto branches, helping them stay safe and reach yummy leaves. Their bodies are just made to do this, so it doesn't make their heads feel funny or tired like it would for us!

title: What is black light and how do we artificially produce it?
text: Okay, imagine light is like a big box of crayons! You have red, blue, green, and all the colors you can see. But there are also some super secret, invisible crayons in that box that our eyes can't quite see, and one of those is "black light"! It's still light, but it's like a special secret light that makes some things glow that don't usually glow in regular light, like your white socks or cool posters. To make this secret black light, grown-ups use a special light bulb, kind of like the ones in your house, but it has a dark, purpley-blue paint on it, like wearing special sunglasses. This paint blocks almost all the bright, regular colors we *can* see, but it lets the invisible black light sneak out, making it look dim and purple, but ready to make your special toys shine!

title: Where does the money to pay off a loan come from?
text: Imagine you want a yummy cookie, but you don't have one right now. Your grown-up might give you a cookie, but you promise to give them one back later when you have one. Where do you get that cookie to give back? Well, when grown-ups go to their jobs, they do important things like helping people or building houses. After they work really hard, their boss gives them special "work money" for all their effort! That's *their own* money they earned. They take some of that money they earned and use it to give back the money they borrowed, just like you'd give back a cookie when you have one. So, the money to pay back a loan comes from the money people earn when they work!

title: Why is it that whenever I go to open a jar I closed, it seems like it was closed with a machine?
text: Okay, imagine your jar is like a little house for air, and when you put the lid on, you trap some air inside. That air likes to stretch out and take up space. But sometimes, when the jar sits there for a bit, especially if it cools down, the air inside gets a tiny, tiny bit squished. And when air gets squished, it pulls the lid down super, super tight, like a big, invisible hug! It's not a machine making it hard to open, it's just the air being strong and holding onto the lid so it doesn't escape.

title: Why does a ball bounce higher when it has more air in it?
text: Imagine the air inside your ball is like a bunch of tiny, invisible springs that want to push out. When your ball hits the ground, it squishes a little, and those springs get squished too! But springs don't like to be squished, so they push back really hard to make the ball jump up. When you put *more* air in the ball, it's like making all those springs super tight and ready to push, push, push! So when the ball hits the ground, all those tight springs push back even *stronger* and *faster*, which makes your ball fly up much, much higher in the air. If there's not much air, the springs are floppy and don't push as hard, so it's not as bouncy.

title: Why do some companies print their products expiration date in code instead of an easy to read format?
text: Imagine you have a secret club, and you have a secret code word only your friends understand. Companies are a bit like that! They have a secret code (that funny mix of numbers and letters) only *they* and the big stores understand. This secret code helps them keep track of *all* their food and toys, like knowing exactly when they made it or which big truck it came on. It helps them make sure they always have the freshest things on the shelf, and they know exactly which old ones to take away. For *you*, they usually put an easy-to-read date, so you know when it's still yummy and safe to eat. The secret code is just for their big, grown-up jobs, not for little super-eaters like you!

title: Why do eggs become solid when we cook them?
text: Imagine an egg is full of super tiny, invisible, wiggly strings that are all floating around loose, making the egg runny and squishy. When you put the egg on the hot stove, the heat is like a magic spell that makes those tiny strings get super excited! They start grabbing onto each other and holding hands really, really tight. Once they're all holding hands and stuck together in a big net, they can't wiggle and slide anymore, so they make a big, solid block, turning the egg from squishy to firm!

title: Why do chefs routinely handle food using their bare hands instead of using gloves? Isn't it unhygenic?
text: Imagine you're building a super cool tower with LEGOs. It's much easier to feel and put the little bricks together with your own fingers, right? Chefs are a bit like that with food! They use their hands to feel the food, mix it just right, and make sure everything is perfect, like having a special superpower for cooking! Now, about yucky germs! Chefs know all about keeping things super clean. They wash their hands with lots of soap and water, like, a *gazillion* times a day – way more than you wash yours before snack time! This makes sure their hands are super clean before they touch the food that's going to be cooked. Sometimes, if the food is already cooked and super yummy and they don't want to touch it with their bare hands (like making your sandwich for school), or if it's really sticky, they might put on a special glove. But for most cooking, super clean bare hands work best because they can feel everything just perfectly!

title: What keeps antarctic penguins from having frostbitten feet?
text: Penguins live where it's super, super cold, but their feet have a special trick! Imagine you have warm juice (that's their warm blood) going down to your feet, and cold juice (that's their cold blood) coming back up. Instead of letting all the warm juice get super cold at their feet, they have the warm juice give some of its warmth to the cold juice on its way back up, before it even gets to the feet! This means the blood that actually goes into their feet is already a little bit cooler, so their feet don't get too hot and lose all that precious warmth to the freezing ice. It's like a clever way to keep their feet just chilly enough to not freeze, but not waste all their body's heat! Plus, their feet don't have lots of squishy parts that need to be super warm anyway.

title: Why do some people have opposite reactions to caffeine and drowsy medicine?
text: Imagine your body is like a special toy robot, and the medicine or drink is like a secret code you give it. For most robots, when you give them the 'caffeine code' (like in coffee), it tells them to wake up and zoom around! title: Why is cold water a more refreshing drink than warm water?
text: Imagine your body is like a little house, and sometimes it gets too warm, especially when you've been playing super hard! When you drink cold water, it's like giving your mouth and tummy a big, cool hug. This cool hug quickly tells your brain, "Hooray! We're getting cooler!" and makes your whole body feel happy and refreshed, like when you jump into a cool swimming pool on a hot day. Warm water is still good for you, but it's more like a gentle pat, and it doesn't send that super-fast "we're cooling down!" message to your brain as strongly. So, the cold water just feels extra special and makes you feel better faster when you're hot and thirsty!

title: How does a hydrofoil ship work and why is it advantageous?
text: Imagine a regular boat is like a big block trying to push through sticky mud – it's slow because the whole big boat body is dragging through the water! A hydrofoil boat has special "wings" attached underneath its tummy, kind of like an airplane has wings in the sky. When this boat starts to go super fast, these underwater wings work like the airplane wings, pushing up on the boat so hard that the whole big boat body actually lifts *out* of the water! Now, only the tiny wings are touching the water, not the big, heavy boat body. This is super good because it means the boat can go much, much faster, because it's not dragging its big tummy through all that sticky water anymore. Plus, because it's floating above the waves instead of bumping and smashing through them, the ride feels much smoother, like you're flying low over the water instead of bouncing around!

title: Why do subscription services like Hulu or Netflix take down titles that are in demand?

text: It can feel really confusing and sad when something so terrible happens, like a grown-up hurting a child. When grown-ups do very bad things, they usually go to a special timeout place called jail. But sometimes, it's not that simple. Imagine if a grown-up got very, very sick in their head, like a bad fever in their brain, so sick they couldn't think straight or understand what they were doing was super wrong. title: Why does water have a blue/green color in oceans, lakes, etc when it is actually clear?
text: Imagine you have a tiny sip of water in a clear cup. It looks clear, right? That's because a little bit of water *is* clear! But when there's a super, super big puddle, like the ocean or a huge lake, it looks blue or green. Here's why: The sun shines light that has all the colors of the rainbow in it, like red, orange, yellow, green, and blue. When this light goes into the big ocean, the water is like a little sponge that soaks up some of those colors. It's really good at soaking up the red, orange, and yellow light! But it's not very good at soaking up the blue and green light. So, when there's a LOT of water, all the red, orange, and yellow light gets soaked up and disappears, and only the blue and green light is left to bounce back to your eyes. That's why the big ocean looks blue or green, even though your little cup of water is clear!

title: What's the history of the prefixes in front of many African American first names?
text: Imagine your favorite toy, but then you add a special sticker or a cool new color to make it *extra* special and just yours! A long, long time ago, when Black families were becoming super strong and proud after some hard times, they wanted to give their babies names that felt extra special and unique to them. They started taking little sounds, like 'La-' (like in LaToya), 'De-' (like in DeShawn), or 'Sha-' (like in Shaquana), and putting them at the beginning of names they liked. It was like adding a special sparkle or a secret code to make the name brand new and just for their child. It showed how creative and unique they were, and it became a special tradition that many families still love to do today to make their children's names wonderfully their own!

title: Why do too sweet or too salty things make us thirsty?
text: Imagine your body is like a big house, and inside are millions of tiny, tiny water balloons! These balloons need to stay full of water to be happy and bouncy. When you eat something super salty, like too many chips, or super sweet, like a giant lollipop, the salt and sugar are like little thirsty magnets that *really* want water. They start to pull a tiny bit of water *out* of your happy water balloons. When your balloons lose some water, they get a little bit sad and squishy, and your body feels it! It then sends a message to your brain that says, "Hey! My water balloons are getting empty! We need more water *right now* to fill them back up!" That's what makes you feel thirsty – your body telling you to drink so your water balloons can be happy and full again!

title: Can you really find someones browsing history through Google?
text: Imagine Google is like a super big, friendly librarian who knows where *all* the books are in the whole world! But your browsing history is like *your own secret diary* of which books *you* looked at on *your* computer. The big librarian (Google) doesn't just tell everyone what's in your secret diary! If *you* are signed into Google (like wearing your special name tag), Google can help *you* remember the places *you* visited, but only *you* can see *your* list. No one else can just ask the big librarian, "Hey, what did [Someone Else] read in their diary?" Google says, "Nope, that's their secret!" So, no, you can't just type someone's name into Google and find their secret browsing history. That's private, like your favorite toy.

title: How do LEDs work?
text: Imagine you have a very special, tiny, tiny light, like a little magic bead! That's an LED. Inside this magic bead, there are two different kinds of super tiny, invisible friends. One kind of friend has extra happy energy, and the other kind of friend is looking for some happy energy. When you give the LED electricity (which is like a super fast stream of invisible power-juice), it pushes the extra-happy friends towards the friends who want happy energy. title: How does an IV drip work? How does the body accept and process that fluid?
text: Imagine your body is like a garden, and sometimes your plants (your body parts) get thirsty or need special food (medicine). When you can't drink water or eat food with medicine, like when your tummy hurts, doctors have a clever trick called an IV drip! It's like this: they put a super tiny, soft straw, called a needle, just for a second, into a little river inside your arm – that river is your blood! Then, they take the needle out and leave a tiny, soft tube. This tube is connected to a bag of special water or medicine that hangs up high, like a balloon. Because it's high up, the water slowly, slowly drips down the tube, right into your blood river. Your body is super smart! It loves this special water because it's just like the water already inside you. The blood river carries this new water all over your body, making your thirsty parts feel much better, much faster than if you just drank it. It's like giving water directly to the roots of a plant! Your body just uses what it needs to feel strong and healthy, and anything extra it doesn't need, it just sends out when you go pee-pee, just like when you drink a lot of juice!

title: If someone was brought up without being told about sex, would they still know what to do?
text: Imagine a little bird. Nobody tells the bird how to build a nest or how to have baby birds, but when it grows up, it just *feels* like it knows what to do because it's a natural part of being a bird. Our bodies are a bit like that too! When people grow big, their bodies start to have natural feelings, like feeling hungry when it's time to eat, or feeling sleepy when it's bedtime. There's also a special grown-up feeling that makes people want to be very close to someone they love. So, they might have a basic *feeling* about what to do because it's a natural grown-up thing, like how a bird knows to build a nest. But knowing how to do it in a very gentle, kind, and safe way, and understanding all the important parts, is something grown-ups learn from talking and being taught, just like we learn how to share toys nicely or cross the road safely.

title: How do they make Gorilla Glass stronger than regular glass?
text: Okay, imagine regular glass is like a wall made of tiny, tiny LEGO bricks, but some of the bricks are a little bit loose, so it's easy to push them apart and break the wall. Now, Gorilla Glass is special! They take that regular glass and give it a super warm bath in a special, magic liquid. In this bath, some of the tiny, weaker LEGO bricks inside the glass get pushed out by bigger, stronger LEGO bricks that want to take their spot. It's like bigger, stronger kids coming to play and pushing the smaller kids to the sides, making everyone inside squish together super tight! Because all the tiny parts inside are so tightly squished and packed together, it makes the glass super, super strong and hard to break, like a really crowded room where it's hard to knock anyone over. So when your grown-up drops their phone, that special glass is much tougher because of all those strong, squished bricks!

title: Who puts together programme schedules? And in the case of 24/7 channels, is it somebody's job to watch TV all night?
text: Imagine TV channels are like a giant toy box, and grown-ups called 'schedulers' are like the people who decide which toy you play with when. They have a big list, like your daily schedule, and they decide 'Okay, cartoons now, then a movie, then the news.' They use special computers to help them remember everything and put it all in the right order. For TV that plays all day and all night, it's not like someone is sitting there watching every single show like you watch your favorite cartoon! Instead, once the schedulers make their big list, a super smart computer takes over. It's like a robot that knows exactly when to start and stop each show, even when everyone is asleep. Sometimes, another grown-up called an 'operator' is there, not watching for fun, but just looking at lots of screens to make sure the clever computer is doing its job right and nothing goes wrong, like the sound breaking or a show not starting on time. So, it's mostly computers doing the work through the night!

title: Why can receipt printers only use thermal paper? What's the difference between receipt printers and regular printers?
text: Imagine a special kind of paper, like a secret drawing paper, that changes color when it gets a little warm. Receipt printers are like magic drawing machines that don't need any ink! Instead, they have a tiny, warm finger inside that touches this special paper. Wherever the warm finger touches, the paper turns dark, making all the words and numbers appear, like magic! That's why they can only use thermal paper – it's the only paper that knows how to do this heat trick. Regular printers are different, like a big painting machine. They use colorful paint, called ink, that squirts onto normal paper to make pictures and words, just like you use crayons on your drawing paper! So, receipt printers are super fast and simple, using heat on special paper, while regular printers use colorful paint on regular paper.

title: Why do we have eyebrows?
text: Eyebrows are like little fuzzy roofs for your eyes! They do two super important jobs. First, imagine if you were playing outside and got all sweaty, or if it started to rain. Your eyebrows catch all the drips and stop them from running right into your eyes, which would make them sting and blurry! They're like tiny little sponges that soak up the water or push it to the side. Second, eyebrows help us show grown-ups how we feel without even talking! When you're surprised, your eyebrows might go way up! When you're thinking hard, they might scrunch together. They help people understand if you're happy, sad, or just thinking about cookies!

title: Why do advertisers allow their commercials to repeat over and over when aired on a steaming device? They must know it enrages their potential customers, right?
text: Imagine you have a super yummy cookie you want all your friends to know about! You might tell them about it, and then tell them again, and again, because you really, really want them to remember it and maybe even want one too. The grown-ups who make commercials are doing a similar thing. They have a special toy, a yummy snack, or a fun movie they want *you* to know about. They pay the TV people lots of money to show their commercial many, many times because they think that even if you get a little bit tired of seeing it, you'll still remember their special thing when you go to the store with your mommy or daddy. They hope that remembering their special thing is more important than you being a little bit grumpy for a moment, because then you might ask for it later!

title: Why Does My shower Curtain Pull Inwards All The Time?
text: Imagine your shower is like a cozy little room! When you turn on the warm water, it makes the air inside your shower warm and happy. This warm air wants to go up and out, like a balloon floating away. As it goes out, the cooler air from your bathroom wants to sneak *into* your shower to fill its spot, and this moving air can gently push your curtain inwards. Also, when the water sprays out of the shower head, it's like a little wind machine inside your shower! This wind makes the air right near the water move super fast. And when air moves super fast, it actually makes a tiny little 'suck' or 'pull' that makes the curtain want to come closer to the water, like it's trying to give the water a hug!

title: Why is the Netflix series: Dear White People so unpopular when it is based on the film Dear White People which is the same premise and popular?
text: Imagine you have a super cool new toy, like a special car! When that car first came out as a movie, it was so exciting because it was new and everyone wanted to see it and talk about it. It was like getting to play with the cool car for a little bit and it felt really special. Then, when they made it into a TV show, it was like getting to play with that *same car* every single day, for a very long time. Even though it's still a cool car, sometimes when you play with something for a long, long time, it doesn't feel as new or as special as when you first saw it. Plus, when something is new, everyone rushes to see it, but when it's been around for a while, people might have already moved on to other new exciting toys. So, even if the show was good, it wasn't as *new* anymore, and maybe some people just liked the shorter playtime with the car better than the very long playtime.

title: Why are most weigh stations on US highways always closed? And what is their intended function in the first place?
text: Imagine big, big trucks carrying lots of toys or food. If a truck carries too many toys, it gets too heavy! If it's too heavy, it can hurt the road, or its wheels might break, which isn't safe. So, a weigh station is like a special doctor's office for big trucks. Trucks drive onto a giant scale, and people check if they are carrying too much weight, and if all their lights and tires are working okay, just like a doctor checks if you're healthy! Now, why do they look closed sometimes? Well, the people who work there need to go home and sleep, just like your mommy and daddy! They can't be there all the time. So, they open up when lots of big trucks are driving around, or when they want to do a special check to make sure everything is super safe. When they're not open, it just means they're taking a break or they're not needed right then, but they'll open again later!

title: How is my nose stuffy and runny at the same time?
text: Imagine your nose is like two little tunnels, and when you get sick, tiny bad guys (germs!) try to get in. Your nose tries really hard to stop them! First, it sends lots of helpers to make the tunnels inside puffier, like when you blow up a balloon a little bit. This makes it hard for air to get through, so it feels stuffy. But at the same time, your nose also makes lots and lots of slippery water, like a tiny waterfall, to try and wash all the bad guys away and push them out. So, you have a puffy tunnel that's hard to breathe through, and lots of watery snot trying to rush out at the same time! It's like a crowded slide that's also super wet.

title: During embryonic development, how do cells "know" which side is the left side of the body versus the right side?
text: Imagine you're building a special toy, like a robot, and you need to make sure its left arm goes on the left side and its right arm goes on the right side. When a baby is just a tiny, tiny speck inside mommy, it has super small building blocks called cells. Right in the middle of these building blocks, there's a special little "fan" that's so small you can't even see it! This fan spins and makes a very gentle current, like a tiny breeze, that pushes some special "sparkle dust" to one side, which becomes the left side. The cells on that side feel the sparkle dust and say, "Oh! This must be the left side, I'll put the heart here!" The other side doesn't feel the sparkle dust as much, so it knows it's the right side and puts other things there. So, the tiny fan and the sparkle dust help all the building blocks know exactly where to go!

title: How can there be more than three dimensions?
text: Okay, imagine you're a little ant walking on a very big, flat drawing, like a picture on the floor. You can go left and right, and you can go up and down on the drawing. Those are two directions, right? But you can't go "up" into the air, because you're flat on the drawing! We, big people, can see you on the drawing, and we can also move up into the air and down to the floor. That's our third direction! So, for the ant, going "up" into the air would be a brand new, amazing direction they can't even imagine. Now, imagine there are even more secret directions, like a super-duper "up" or a totally different "sideways" that *we* can't see or move into, but they might still be there, just waiting for us to figure out how to go that way! It's like finding a secret path no one knew about before.

title: Why do I see silver bacteria like lines running around my environment when I rub my eyes too hard?
text: You know how sometimes when you rub your eyes really, really hard, you see little sparkly lines or squiggles dancing around, almost like tiny silver worms? Those aren't real things floating in your room or actual little bugs! Your eye is like a super special camera that helps you see everything. When you rub it hard, you're actually giving that camera a little squeeze. That squeeze makes the camera get a tiny bit confused for a moment, and it sends funny signals to your brain that look like those sparkly lines or lights. It's like when you press on your TV screen and see weird colors for a second – the screen isn't broken, it just got a little poke! Your eye camera is just saying 'Whoa, what was that?' for a moment, and then it goes back to normal when you stop rubbing. So, those lines are just your eye's way of saying 'Hey, I just got a big hug!'

title: Why do female kangeroos have 3 vaginas?
text: Imagine your house has special doors for different things! Girl kangaroos are a bit like that with their special 'tunnels' inside. They actually have three of these paths. Two of them are like exit doors just for their super tiny babies to come out. Kangaroo babies are born extra, extra small, like a jelly bean, and use one of these paths to quickly crawl all the way into their mom's warm pouch, which is like a built-in pocket on her tummy. The third path is for when the mommy kangaroo mates with a daddy kangaroo, which is how the baby gets started in the first place! So, it's not really three 'vaginas' like we think of, but more like a special arrangement of three tunnels that help them make and have their super little babies that then grow big and strong inside their pouch.

title: Why is Golf the go to sports for rich and/or powerful people like Presidents, CEOs? What is special about it?
text: Imagine you have a super important secret club, and you want to talk about big grown-up stuff, like how to make more toys or build a super tall tower. Golf is like that! It takes a super long time to play, like a whole afternoon, so important grown-ups can spend lots and lots of time together just walking and talking slowly. They're not running super fast or shouting, so it's quiet and they can hear each other really well. Plus, the big green fields are far away from other people, like a secret garden, so they can talk about their big plans or make new friends who can help them with their important jobs, all without lots of ears listening in. It's like a long, calm walk and talk meeting where you also get to hit a little ball!

title: Why does looking at somebody else's wounds or injuries cause me to feel disgusted/uncomfortable?
text: You know how sometimes when you see a big boo-boo on your friend, like a scraped knee or a cut, it makes your tummy feel a little funny or makes you want to look away? That's actually your super-duper clever body trying to tell you something! It's like your own special alarm system inside your head. When you see someone else's owie, your brain goes, "Whoa! That looks like it hurts, and maybe there are tiny invisible yucky bugs (we call them germs!) that could make someone sick." Your body wants to keep you safe and healthy, so that funny feeling is its way of saying, "Be careful! Let's stay away from things that could make *us* get a boo-boo too, or get sick from those yucky bugs." It also sometimes makes you want to help your friend feel better, because your heart is kind. So, it's a helpful feeling that keeps you safe and reminds you to be careful!

title: Why are there always chunks of rubber on the side of the highway?
text: You know how your shoes have a bottom part that touches the ground when you run? Cars have special big, black, round 'shoes' called tires! When cars drive super, super fast for a very, very long time, especially when it's hot outside, their tires get really, really warm, just like your feet get warm when you run a lot. Sometimes, if a tire gets too old or too hot, or if it hits something sharp, a little piece of that black squishy 'shoe skin' can decide it doesn't want to be on the tire anymore and pops right off! Because the car is going so fast, that little piece of rubber flies way over to the side of the road and just stays there, waiting for someone to pick it up, like a lost toy that flew off your wagon.

title: Why in the solar system planets are so different from each other?
text: Imagine our whole solar system started like a giant messy room with lots and lots of tiny space dust and rocks, like tiny LEGOs! Our Sun is like a giant, super-hot lightbulb in the middle. Now, because some planets were built **very close to the hot Sun**, it was too hot for light, fluffy gas to stick around. So, these planets, like Earth, Mars, Venus, and Mercury, ended up being smaller and made mostly of hard rock, like strong little LEGO bricks. But the planets that were built **very far away from the hot Sun** were super cold! Out there, all the light, fluffy gas could easily stick together with the rocks, making them grow super, super big and puffy, like giant gas balloons! That's why planets like Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune are huge and mostly made of gas. Also, some planets just gathered more space stuff than others

title: How come when someone has a very bad cold, they feel even worse at night?

title: Why is it recommended that new mobile phones be charged 6-8 hours before use?
text: That's a super interesting question, but it's like asking why we have to wait for the milkman to deliver milk when we can just get it from the store now! A long, long time ago, when phones were much older and their batteries were different (like old-fashioned toys), it was thought that a very long first charge, like 6 to 8 hours, would help the battery learn to be strong and last longer. It was kind of like teaching a brand new puppy how to eat its food properly. But new phones today are super smart and have much newer, better batteries! Their batteries are like little energy cups that already know exactly what to do. You don't need to charge them for a super long time before you play. You can just plug it in until it's full, like when your juice cup is full, and then you can start playing right away! It's actually better for these new smart batteries if you don't wait for them to be totally, totally empty or keep them plugged in for too, too long after they're already full.

title: Why does water form into droplets as its smallest unit? What's special about that specific size?

If they spread out flat, too many friends would be on the edge and not get as many hugs. So, a water droplet is just a big group of water friends all hugging each other into the best, tightest little ball they can make!

title: Why do we still have to file taxes?
text: Imagine all the grown-ups in our town put a little bit of their money, like their allowance, into a really, really big jar. It's just a way to make sure everyone's helping fairly, and that the big jar always has enough money for all the important things we need as a community.

title: Why are all watches set to 10:09 in adverts?
text: Imagine your toy box, and you want to show off your favorite toy – you'd put it in a way that looks the best, right? title: If you get water on something like clothing, how come it becomes darker?
text: Imagine your shirt is like a lot of tiny, tiny hills and valleys. When light (like from the sun or a lamp) hits your dry shirt, it bounces off all those tiny hills and goes right into your eyes, so you see its color. But when your shirt gets wet, the water fills up all those tiny hills and valleys, making the top of your shirt much smoother, like a calm lake. Now, when the light hits the wet, smooth part, some of it goes *into* the water and gets a little bit trapped, instead of bouncing back to your eyes right away. Since less light bounces straight back to your eyes, your shirt looks darker, almost like a shadow. It's still the same color, but the water makes it look a little bit shy because it's holding onto some of the light!

title: Are there any biological advantages to being overweight? Could it allow you to survive longer without food?
text: Imagine your body is like a toy car, and food is the special battery it needs to run and play! So, yes, having those extra squishy bits means your body has more stored-up energy, like a backup battery, which can help you survive a little longer if there's no food around to give it new energy.

text: Imagine some people are put into a super, super cold bed, like a giant freezer, hoping to wake up in the future when doctors are super smart. It's like they're taking a very, very long nap. title: How do cotton candy machines work?
text: Imagine you have special sparkly sugar, like tiny little crystals! You put this sugar into a super-duper fast spinning bowl inside the machine. As these little bits of hot, gooey sugar fly out into the air, they cool down super, super fast! When they cool down that quickly, they stretch out into the thinnest, fluffiest, melt-in-your-mouth threads, just like a spider's web, but made of sweet, yummy sugar! Then, you just twirl a stick around to catch all those magical, sugary threads, and *poof* – you have cotton candy!

title: Green, red, yellow and so on are colours. Black and white aren't. So why aren't they and what are they then?

When something is white, it's sending *all* the color messages at once, like a big, bright party of all the colors together! That's why it looks so bright. But when something is black, it's not sending *any* color messages at all. It's like the lights are off and no colors are coming back to your eyes, because it just soaks up all the light. So white is when you see *all* the colors, and black is when you see *no* colors. They're special because they are about having *all* or *none* of the light messages!

title: Why does one get heavy sweating before getting healed from a fever?
text: Okay, imagine your body is like a little house, and sometimes bad guys (germs) try to get in and make you sick. When you have a fever, your house (your body) turns up the heat, like a super warm oven, to try and cook those bad guys away and make them leave! It's working super hard to fight them. After your body has won the fight and kicked the bad guys out, it's still super hot from all that hard work. So, your body has a special way to cool down, like turning on a little sprinkler system inside you! That's the sweat. When the water (sweat) comes out and then dries, it takes all the extra heat with it, making you feel cooler and much better. So, you sweat a lot because your body is saying, "Phew, I won! Now let's cool down and get back to normal!"

title: Why are people in the US allowed to open credit cards under their children's names?
text: Imagine a credit card is like a special grown-up ticket that lets you buy toys now and your mommy or daddy pays for them later. Sometimes, a grown-up might add their child's name to their own ticket. It's not really *your* ticket to go buy all the candy you want, but it's like your grown-up is saying, "See? title: Why does being hungry make you angry?
text: Imagine your body is like a super cool toy car, and food is the special fuel that makes it zoom and play! When your car runs out of fuel, it gets stuck and can't do anything, right? And sometimes, when we feel tired or our body feels uncomfortable, it makes us feel grumpy and a bit angry, just like when you're super sleepy and don't want to share your favorite toy. But don't worry, a yummy snack or meal makes everything feel much better!

title: How does absorbed light turn into heat? This makes no sense.
text: Okay, imagine light is like super tiny, super fast bouncy balls! And everything around you, like your toy car or your sweater, is made of even tinier little LEGO bricks that are stuck together. When those super fast bouncy balls (light) hit the LEGO bricks in your toy car, they don't always bounce off. Sometimes, they get *stuck* to the LEGO bricks, and when they do, they make those LEGO bricks jiggle and shake really, really fast! It's like when you run around a lot, you get warm, right? Well, when all those tiny LEGO bricks inside your toy car start jiggling and shaking super fast because of the light, that jiggling and shaking is what we feel as heat! So, the light energy gets turned into jiggling energy, and jiggling energy makes things warm.

title: Why have humans adapted to like sweet or salty things better than bitter, sour, etc. things?
text: Imagine your body is like a little car that needs special fuel to run and play all day! **Sweet things** are like super good fuel! When you taste something sweet, like a yummy cookie or a juicy apple, your body says, "Yay! This has lots of energy to help me run, jump, and learn!" Sweet usually means it's safe to eat and gives you power. **Salty things** are also important, but in a different way. It's like a special ingredient your body needs a little bit of to work properly, just like a car needs a little bit of oil. Not too much, but just enough to keep everything going smoothly. Your body says, "Oh, a little bit of this salt helps me stay healthy!" Now, **bitter and sour things** are like a little warning signal! If something tastes really bitter, your body might think, "Uh oh, maybe this isn't good for me, it could be a yucky plant that makes me sick!" And if something tastes super sour, like a lemon that's gone bad, your body might think, "Yikes, this might be rotten and make my tummy hurt!" So, your tongue is like a little helper that tastes things and tells your brain, "Hey, this one is good for us!" or "Hmm, maybe let's not eat too much of this one, just to be safe!" It's all to help you pick the best foods to grow big and strong and stay safe!

title: Why the Bulgarian lev (national currency) is allways 1 lev = 0,5 euro? Isn't the same thing as having the euro?
text: Imagine the Bulgarian lev is like a special toy coin, and the Euro is like a grown-up coin. The people in charge of Bulgaria made a super important rule a long, long time ago: their special toy coin, the lev, will *always* be worth exactly half of the grown-up Euro coin. It's like if you had a favorite toy car, and you made a rule that it's always worth two of your friend's toy cars – it never changes! They do this because it makes everyone feel safe and trust the lev. People know exactly what it's worth, so its value doesn't jump up and down like a bouncy ball, which helps everyone buy and sell things easily. It's not *exactly* the same as just having the Euro because Bulgaria still gets to print its own lev money and has to follow special grown-up rules and steps to eventually be able to use the Euro money for real, like passing a big test. So, they have their own money, but it's like it has a super strong invisible string connecting its value to the Euro.

title: How come the North Pole is considered the "Top of the World" and the South Pole, the bottom?
text: Imagine our Earth is like a big, round ball that spins around and around! When grown-ups draw pictures of our Earth, like maps you see in books, they decided a very long time ago to always put the part where the polar bears live (that's the North Pole!) at the very top of the drawing. And the part where the penguins live (that's the South Pole!) always goes at the very bottom. It's just like when you draw a person, you always put their head at the top and their feet at the bottom, right? It helps everyone know which way is which when they look at a map, but in outer space, there isn't really an "up" or "down" for our big Earth ball!

title: How do emotions work?
text: Your head has a super special thinking machine called your brain, kind of like the boss of your whole body! This brain helps you think and move, but it also helps you feel all sorts of things inside, like happy, sad, mad, or scared. When something happens, like getting a yummy cookie or seeing a big, loud truck, your brain quickly figures it out and sends a special message that makes you feel a certain way. So, if you get a cookie, your brain says, "Yummy! Happy!" and you smile. If you fall down, your brain might say, "Ouch! Sad!" and you cry a little. These feelings are like little messages that tell you about the world around you and help you know what's good or what you need to be careful about. All your feelings are important and okay to have!

title: How can someone increase their IQ?
text: Imagine your brain is like a little muscle, just like the ones in your arms and legs! When you play and run, your leg muscles get stronger. Your brain works kind of the same way. When you learn new things, like reading a new book, or trying a new puzzle, or even asking lots of 'why?' questions, your brain gets stronger and better at thinking. Eating yummy, healthy food and getting lots of sleep also helps your brain be super-duper ready to learn. So, to make your brain smarter, just keep learning, playing, asking questions, and taking good care of yourself!

title: What, exactly, is a "bit", as in the fact that the Nintendo 64 was "64 bit"?
text: Imagine you have a tiny little light switch. It can either be ON or OFF, right? That's what a "bit" is, like one tiny light switch in the computer's brain. Now, if you have lots and lots of these tiny light switches, you can make them turn on and off in different patterns, and the computer understands what those patterns mean. When we say the Nintendo 64 was "64-bit", it means it had a super long row of 64 of these little light switches that it could look at all at once! Having more switches means the computer can think about bigger numbers, like counting much, much higher, or understand bigger, more complicated instructions all at the same time. It's like having a really big crayon box with 64 crayons you can use together to draw a much more detailed picture, instead of just a tiny box with only a few crayons.

title: How breaking a company apart and selling pieces can be more profitable than selling it whole?
text: Imagine you have a big toy box with lots of different toys inside: some cool race cars, some pretty dolls, and some building blocks. If you try to sell the *whole toy box* to one friend, maybe they only really like the race cars, so they might not offer much money for the whole thing because they don't care about the dolls or blocks. But what if you take all the toys *out* of the box? You can sell the race cars to your friend who LOVES race cars for a good price, then sell the dolls to another friend who LOVES dolls for another good price, and the blocks to a third friend who LOVES blocks for a third good price. When you add up all the money you got from selling them separately, it's often much, much more than what the first friend offered for the whole mixed-up box! Companies are sometimes like that big toy box – they have different parts that are super special on their own, but when they're all together, people don't always see how valuable each piece truly is. So, breaking them apart lets you sell each special piece to someone who really wants it, and they'll pay more for just that piece, making more money in total.

title: Why does the government tax the money it gives you? (Other than "because it can")
text: Imagine the government is like a big grown-up who takes care of everyone in our town. Sometimes, they give you some money, maybe to help your family buy food or pay for things. But the government also needs money to do important jobs for *everyone*, like building roads so you can drive your car or ride your bike, paying for doctors at the hospital to make you feel better, or making sure there are schools where you can learn. So, when they give you money, they take a tiny little bit back, like a small 'thank you' coin, and put it into their big piggy bank. That way, they have enough money to pay for all those important things that help *all* the people in our town, not just you, and keep everything working nicely!

title: What makes some chocolates taste smoother than others?

That's because the chocolate makers grind it for a very, very long time, making all the chocolate pieces tiny, tiny, tiny.
